title: How to Prep Print Files for Subliminator Orders Without Color Complaints
excerpt: All-over-print failures happen at the file stage, not the press. This checklist covers resolution, bleed, safe zones, and color profiles so your sublimation orders ship right the first time.
body: All-over-print is unforgiving because the artwork covers the entire garment, seams included. A small mistake that would be invisible on a chest print becomes a visible seam mismatch or a white crease under the arm. Most of those failures are locked in before the order is placed, at the file stage, which is also the cheapest place to fix them. The good news is that file problems are almost entirely preventable with a short checklist. The Print-on-Demand category at /category/pod keeps the current shortlist with ratings and pricing for sublimation suppliers.

Resolution comes first. Design at final print size rather than designing small and scaling up, because upscaling creates soft edges that show badly on large panels. Work at three hundred pixels per inch at the actual dimensions of the print sheet, and keep your source file layered so a revision does not mean starting over. If you are building repeating patterns, tile the artwork and inspect the seam where the pattern meets itself before you export, because a visible repeat line is the most common complaint on all-over garments.

Bleed and safe zones matter more here than on any other product. Sublimation prints onto a flat panel that is then cut and sewn, so anything close to an edge can be trimmed or swallowed by a seam. Extend artwork past the trim line and keep logos, faces, and text away from underarm seams, side seams, and the waistband. Mockups often hide this problem: a flat preview looks clean while the finished garment splits a word across two panels that never line up in real life.

Color is where disputes start. Screens are backlit and fabric is not, so a bright design on a monitor prints noticeably darker on polyester. Design in the color profile your supplier specifies, soft-proof against it, and accept that neon tones and deep navy are the hardest to reproduce. If an exact brand color matters, order a physical sample on the same blank and compare it under normal indoor light, then adjust the file once rather than arguing about every batch after it ships.

Build a repeatable export routine. Save a template with the correct dimensions, profile, bleed, and naming convention, and use it for every design so nothing ships from a one-off export. Name files by product and variant rather than by design name, because all-over garments usually need different files for each size. Keep a folder of approved files with a short note on what each one is for, so a freelancer or assistant can produce new designs without relearning your rules from scratch.

Finally, order your own product. The only way to know whether a file works is to hold the finished garment, stretch the seams, and wash it. Check that panels line up, colors hold, and there are no white creases where the fabric folded during pressing. Fix the file, not the listing, because a rewritten description will not save a bad seam. You can find current product dimensions, file requirements, and pricing on the Subliminator page at /tool/subliminator, and compare other sublimation suppliers in the Print-on-Demand category at /category/pod.
